I can't say I fully agree.

I have issues with Twitter, and some of those issues involve the verified check system. But I don't think the importance of a valid verified check depends purely on the nu ber of people who may be interested in the verification.

The issue is more a matter of whether people would have an interest in identifying whether a person is really who they claim. By that standard, the people named probably qualify. I wouldn't though. The people who would care know me in real life anyway. To the people who otherwise interact with me on Twitter it doesn't really matter if the name on my account is really mine or made up (it happens to be real but that isn't important). It is an account with which they interact and it is consistent in its views and humor, so who is behind it in real life is immaterial.

The problems I see are twofld.

First, they began using the system as a reward system for the verified person ignoring the users for whom it is useful and the only real reason for it. An example of this was removing @Nero's check mark because he engaged in wrongthink.

Second, by basically allowing anyone to get a check mark, they've made it possible to create the confusion which the marks were meant to negate. It is not as though everyone has a unique name. Many people share names. Also, it is not a hard system to game if people are inclined.

Twitter has horrible customer service and makes really bad business decisions. It's a shame because it can serve as a decent platform for disseminating news and other things.

Granted, those are logical arguments, and I don't disagree.

My assertion is that their original method of handing it out actually made some form of sense and while not a stellar idea, at least it was an above average one by their usual track record which they recently threw away, though the business with Milo definitely did start their trend of turning the verified tag into the parody it is now.
